newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Somali factions warn Aideed against any attack.
newsitem.headline: Somali factions warn Aideed against any attack.

text.p: Somali faction leaders vowed on Monday to fight back if attacked after a powerful faction led by Hussein Aideed blasted them for an Ethiopian-backed peace agreement.
North Mogadishu faction leader Ali Mahdi Mohamed said though Hussein Aideed refused to attend talks between the 26 factions in Ethiopia they had left the door open in case he changed his mind.
"But this does not mean that if there is aggression against one of them they will be deprived of the right of self defence," said Ali Mahdi, who is also a self-styled president of Somalia.

"If there is any attack on one of the 26 faction leaders who signed the reconciliation process it will be considered an attack on all of them and the response will be collective," he told a news conference.
Mohamed Kanyare Afrah, interior minister in Aideed's self-styled government, said earlier on Monday he would arrest all those at the talks in Ethiopia and charge them with treason.

Afrah, of the Murusade sub-clan, said the conference in Ethiopia between the Somali factions was designed to break up Somalia and the peace talks were no difference from the Berlin Conference of 1884 that divided Africa among colonial powers.

Most of the faction leaders who met in Ethiopia never travel through territory controlled by Aideed but some smaller groups such as a wing of the Murusade represented at the talks could be affected by the threat.
Aideed, a south Mogadishu faction leader and 34-year-old former U.S. marine, succeeded his father Mohamed Aideed at his death last August and was elected president by his supporters.
Aideed refused to attend the Ethiopian-backed peace talks as the other factions flatly refuse to recognise him as president of Somalia or the authority of his south Mogadishu government.
After eight weeks of talks, the 26 factions in Addis Ababa said on Friday they were setting up a National Salvation Council authorised to establish a provisional central government.
The leaders appealed to Aideed and Mohamed Egal, leader of the self-declared Somaliland republic, to participate in talks.
The factions said all groups would be invited to a national reconciliation conference in Somalia to discuss the approval of a charter for a provisional central government. No date was set.
Somalia has had no central government since 1991 when rebels ousted late president Mohammed Siad Barre but turned their guns against each other and divided the country into rival fiefdoms.
In Addis Ababa on Monday the allied faction leaders urged the Somali Moslem fundamentalist group al-Ittihad al-Islam "to refrain from violence which disturbs the peace of the region".
Ali Mahdi said al-Ittihad was "a terrorist group which has no legality whatsoever" and said the 26 leaders were aware the group was aided by foreign countries but declined to name them.
Al-Ittihad has called a "jihad" or holy war against Ethiopian forces which thrust into southwest Somalia last month. Ethiopia said it beat back Moslem fundamentalists attacking a border town.

It was the second time in five months Ethiopia sent troops into Somalia against al-Ittihad. Last August Addis Ababa said its forces had killed more than 230 fighters of a group which with foreign backing had mounted attacks inside Ethiopia.
